notes.meaning: The writer's heart overflows with excitement because he has a grand theme about the king. His thoughts are so stirred by God's Spirit that his tongue speaks as smoothly and quickly as a practiced scribe writing on parchment. This joyful song points beyond ordinary royalty to King Jesus and His kingdom.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some early church teachers read the opening line about the heart uttering a good word as God the Father speaking of the eternal generation of the Son, the Word.

notes.meaning: The king is praised as the most handsome of men, possessing a moral beauty and perfection that exceeds all others. His speech is filled with divine grace, bringing comfort, wisdom, and truth to all who listen. Because God has set His eternal favor on Him, His blessings will never end.

The king is summoned to strap on his royal sword and ride out to battle in glorious majesty. He does not ride for personal fame or cruel conquest, but to defend truth, humble meekness, and righteousness. His sharp arrows pierce the hearts of His enemies, causing people and nations to fall before Him either in humble repentance or under divine judgment.

The king is directly addressed as God, showing that this eternal ruler is the divine Messiah. While all human empires crumble, His throne will never pass away, and His scepter always rules with total justice.

differ.view: Some Anglicans prefer to translate the phrase as 'Your throne is of God,' seeing the verse as originally describing an earthly king who pointed forward to Christ.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars render the words as 'your divine throne' or 'God has enthroned you,' understanding them as courtly language for an earthly king rather than a direct claim of deity in the original setting.

notes.meaning: Because this King completely loves what is right and detests what is evil, God honors Him above all others. He is anointed with the oil of joy, receiving the fullness of the Holy Spirit beyond any other priest, prophet, or ruler. Jesus bore suffering on earth and was raised to supreme gladness at the Father's right hand.

The King prepares for His royal wedding in robes scented with sweet and costly perfumes. Music from palaces richly decorated with ivory rings out to welcome Him and make Him glad. These beautiful scents and sounds reflect the perfection of Christ and the great joy of heaven.

Royal women attend the court, while the bride stands in the place of highest honor at the king's right hand. She is beautifully dressed in robes adorned with the finest gold of Ophir. This scene pictures the Church standing close to Christ, clothed in the precious honor He provides.

differ.view: Some Anglicans see the queen at the right hand as the Jewish people restored to God in the future, while the attending royal daughters represent Gentile churches.

notes.meaning: The bride is gently urged to listen, look, and pay close attention to wise counsel. She must leave behind her former home and old loyalties to dedicate herself entirely to her husband. When she offers this wholehearted devotion, the king delights in her beauty, and she honors and worships Him as her lord.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: The call for the daughter to listen and incline her ear is used in church services as a liturgical verse honoring Mary, the mother of Jesus.

notes.meaning: The wealthy sea city of Tyre sends tribute, and the richest people come asking for the bride's favor. Her union with the king brings respect and honor from surrounding nations. In the same way, when people turn to Christ, the nations gladly bring their lives and treasures to serve His kingdom.

The royal bride waits within her chamber, glowing with splendor in a gown woven with gold thread. Her glory is not just skin-deep; her inner character is pure and pleasing to the king. This reminds believers that God values inward holiness of the heart just as much as outward good works.

Dressed in richly embroidered clothing, the bride is escorted to the king alongside her joyful bridesmaids. The entire procession moves forward with celebration until they enter the royal palace. This points ahead to the last day, when Christ will welcome His redeemed people into the everlasting joy of heaven.

The song turns back to the king with a promise of a lasting legacy. Instead of looking back to ancestors, his marriage will produce sons who will rule as princes across the earth. For Christ, this is fulfilled in a vast family of believers from every land who share in His kingdom.

The psalmist vows to keep the king's name alive through every coming age. Because of who He is and what He has done, people from all nations will praise Him forever and ever. God ensures that the honor of Christ will never fade from the earth.
